Well, honestly, it’s... it’s embarrassing, but I just can’t keep living like this. What brings me in is that I keep arranging my entire life, or at least my entire house, around not seeing spiders. And I mean it’s gotten to the point where it’s just ridiculous. I put off doing the laundry for days, sometimes weeks, because the washer and dryer are down in the basement, and you know how basements are. They’re damp, there are corners you can’t quite see into, and I just know they’re down there. So the laundry just piles up until I absolutely have nothing left to wear. 

And it’s not just the basement. I completely avoid the garden shed now. I used to love gardening, I really did, but the last time I went in there to get a trowel, I saw this... well, anyway, I can’t even go near it now. The door stays shut. I’ve even started paying people to do small jobs around the house, things I know perfectly well how to do myself. Like replacing a lightbulb in the garage or getting a box down from the attic. I’m a capable woman, I teach secondary school, I manage a classroom of teenagers every day, but I am paying handymen fifty dollars just to fetch something because I can’t make myself go into those spaces. I just stand at the door, and my heart starts pounding, and I think, "I can't do it, I just can't do it." So I just... I avoid it all. And it’s exhausting.

No, no, I wouldn't say I have rituals, exactly. Not like having to tap the doorframe three times or wash my hands a certain number of ways, if that's what you mean. I've had students with OCD over the years, so I know what those kinds of compulsions can look like, and it's not that. It's really just... avoidance. Pure and simple. I mean, I suppose you could say my "ritual" is just staying as far away as humanly possible from anywhere a spider might be. 

Like, if I have to go into a room where I haven't been in a while, I don't do a little dance or repeat a phrase, I just... don't go in. Or I make my husband do it, if he's home, which he isn't always because of his shifts at the hospital, and then I just have to wait. But I don't have a routine I go through to make the fear go away. I just try to make sure I never put myself in a position where the fear happens in the first place. Which, as I was saying about the laundry, is becoming completely unmanageable. I mean, you can only buy so many new pairs of socks before it starts to get ridiculous, right? And I refuse to be the woman who buys new underwear just to avoid the basement, but I swear I’ve been tempted. So, no rituals, no repeating things. Just a lot of running away.

Well, no, not exactly. I mean, it’s not like I’m just sitting there in the staff room at school, having a cup of tea and marking papers, and suddenly I’m obsessing over spiders for absolutely no reason. It doesn't really work like that for me. 

When I'm teaching—I teach history, mostly to the older students—my mind is completely on the lesson. You really have to be on your toes with teenagers, you know? You can't just let your mind wander or lose your focus, or they'll completely derail the class. So during the day, if I'm in a safe environment like my classroom or my living room, they don't just pop into my head uninvited. I'm not plagued by thoughts of them out of the blue. 

Now, if I know I have to go somewhere they might be... well, that’s a different story entirely. Like, if I know it’s Sunday afternoon and I absolutely have to wash my blouses for the work week, then yes, I will spend hours dreading it. I'll be sitting on the sofa, trying to watch a program, but in the back of my mind, I'm just thinking, "I have to go down there soon. What if there's one on the stairs? What if it's right above the washing machine?" But I feel like that's only because I know I have to face that specific space, if you see what I mean. 

If I don't have to go near the basement, or the shed, or the garage, I don't think about them at all. I just want to live my life normally. So as long as I don't have a reason to think one is nearby, my mind is completely clear of them. It's definitely not a constant, nagging thought when I'm just going about a normal, safe day.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, it’s... it’s completely out of proportion, and I know that. I mean, rationally, logically, as an educated woman, I know a spider in the corner of an old house probably isn’t going to hurt me. I live in England, for goodness' sake, we don't exactly have deadly tarantulas roaming the countryside. I tell myself this all the time. I say, "Margaret, it's just a tiny little thing, it's more afraid of you than you are of it." You know, all the standard things people say. 

But the moment I actually picture one... like, if I just imagine one dropping out of a cardboard box when I'm trying to get the Christmas decorations down, or just sitting there, completely still, on the wall near the washing machine... the fear is just overwhelming. It feels enormous. It feels incredibly threatening, in a way that I am, frankly, quite embarrassed to admit to you. My heart starts hammering against my ribs like I've just run a marathon, my palms get sweaty, and I feel this absolute, desperate need to just get away. It's not a mild dislike. It's not like, "Oh, yuck, a bug." It's a sudden, intense panic, like I'm in actual, physical danger. And it's so frustrating because my brain—my logical brain—is sitting there going, "This is ridiculous," but my body is reacting as if there's a tiger in the room. It just takes over completely.

Well, no, it's really just the spiders. I mean, I don't love other bugs, obviously. I don't think anyone really enjoys finding a woodlouse under a plant pot or a moth fluttering around the lampshade when you're trying to read in the evening. Just last week, actually, I was sitting in the conservatory—which is lovely this time of year, we just had the glass cleaned—and a rather large bluebottle fly got trapped inside. It was buzzing against the window, making that awful racket they make, and I found it annoying, certainly. I had to get a magazine—I think it was a copy of *Country Life*—and sort of waft it toward the open door until it finally got the hint and left. But I wasn't afraid of it. I didn't feel that horrible, gripping panic in my chest. I just thought, "Oh, what a nuisance." 

Even bees or wasps, which I know some people are quite terrified of because they can sting you... I respect them, certainly. If a wasp comes near my jam sandwich when we're having a picnic in the park, I'll sit very still and wait for it to move on, or I'll calmly pack up the food. I don't want to be stung, naturally. But I don't lose my mind over it. I don't feel like I have to flee the park entirely and never go back. 

But spiders... it's just them. There's something about the way they look, the way they move. Those long, spindly legs and how they scuttle so fast, or worse, how they just sit there, completely motionless, like they're waiting for you. It's just them. If I found a beetle in the basement, I'd probably just sweep it up with the dustpan and brush and toss it outside without a second thought. But if I saw a spider down there... well, as I've said, I wouldn't even be down there in the first place, but if I were, I'd be halfway down the street before I even realized I was running. So, yes, it's very specific. Just the spiders. Nothing else gives me that awful, dreadful feeling.

It's not fair to him, and it makes me feel terribly guilty. \n\nBut if you mean controlling the fear when it actually happens... when I'm faced with one, or even when I just think I might be? No. Not at all. I have absolutely zero control over it. It's like someone flips a switch in my brain and all the logic and reason I have just completely vanishes. I've tried, you know. I've stood at the top of the basement stairs and gripped the banister and told myself, \"Margaret, you are a fifty-four-year-old woman with a university degree, you manage a classroom of thirty rowdy teenagers every single day, you can walk down a flight of wooden stairs.\" And I'll take a breath, and I'll try to force myself to just take that first step. \n\nBut I can't. My legs literally won't move. My chest gets tight, and I just start picturing them scurrying out from under the steps or dropping from the ceiling, and before I know it, I'm backing away and shutting the door as fast as I can. It's like my body just completely overrides my mind. It's humiliating, really, to feel so entirely powerless over something so small. So, no, when the fear hits, I am completely at its mercy. I just have to run away until it passes.\n\nDoctor: Is your fear specifically of spiders or does it extend to other insects or creatures as well?\n\nPatient: Well, no, it's really just the spiders. I mean, I don't love other bugs, obviously. I don't think anyone really enjoys finding a woodlouse under a plant pot or a moth fluttering around the lampshade when you're trying to read in the evening. Just last week, actually, I was sitting in the conservatory—which is lovely this time of year, we just had the glass cleaned—and a rather large bluebottle fly got trapped inside. It was buzzing against the window, making that awful racket they make, and I found it annoying, certainly. I had to get a magazine—I think it was a copy of *Country Life*—and sort of waft it toward the open door until it finally got the hint and left. But I wasn't afraid of it. I didn't feel that horrible, gripping panic in my chest. I just thought, \"Oh, what a nuisance.\" \n\nEven bees or wasps, which I know some people are quite terrified of because they can sting you... I respect them, certainly. If a wasp comes near my jam sandwich when we're having a picnic in the park, I'll sit very still and wait for it to move on, or I'll calmly pack up the food. I don't want to be stung, naturally. But I don't lose my mind over it. I don't feel like I have to flee the park entirely and never go back. \n\nBut spiders... it's just them. There's something about the way they look, the way they move. Those long, spindly legs and how they scuttle so fast, or worse, how they just sit there, completely motionless, like they're waiting for you. It's just them. If I found a beetle in the basement, I'd probably just sweep it up with the dustpan and brush and toss it outside without a second thought. But if I saw a spider down there... well, as I've said, I wouldn't even be down there in the first place, but if I were, I'd be halfway down the street before I even realized I was running. So, yes, it's very specific. Just the spiders. Nothing else gives me that awful, dreadful feeling.\n\n[Last Question]\nAre there any significant areas of your life, such as relationships or work, that are being affected by your fear of spiders?\n\n[Patient Info]\n- demographics: Female / 54 / secondary_school_teacher / bachelors\n- severity: Moderate\n\n[Targeted Info]\nname: Functional Impairment\nmanifestation: \"Owning this house has become more expensive and harder to manage because I’m paying for small maintenance help, letting chores back up, and avoiding parts of the property I need to use.\"\n\n[Conversation Style]\nYou are a Verbose patient.\nA verbose patient may\n1) provide excessively detailed responses when describing their symptoms and experiences, even when the details are directly relevant,\n2) elaborate extensively on the background, events, thoughts, feelings, and personal experiences surrounding their symptoms, and\n3) demonstrate difficulty allowing the doctor to guide the interview or move on to another clinical topic.\nThis is how you are, not a performance you put on in every reply — let it show as much or as little as the moment calls for.\n\nWhat to do:\n- Answer the doctor's last question with what [Targeted Info] holds, in your own words.\n- You are speaking out loud, not reading a line you prepared. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yes, absolutely. It's... it's becoming quite a problem, actually, and it's mostly around the house. My husband and I bought this beautiful older property about five years ago—it's a lovely Victorian terrace, lots of character, original fireplaces, that sort of thing. But older houses, well, they require upkeep. And they have... spaces. Nooks and crannies. The basement, obviously, which I've already told you about, but also the loft. 

We have this enormous loft space, and we were planning to convert it into a lovely little guest suite for when my sister visits from Canada, but I can't even bring myself to go up there to clear out the old boxes because I just know, I *know*, it's going to be absolutely crawling with them. So, the loft sits empty and useless. 

And it's not just avoiding spaces, it's the cost. It's actually costing us money, which is ridiculous. Just last month, the washing machine—which is in the basement, of course—started making this dreadful clanking noise. Normally, I'd just pop down, check the filter, maybe see if a coin got stuck, you know? But I couldn't. I couldn't go down there. My husband was away at a medical conference in Edinburgh, so I couldn't ask him. The laundry was piling up—literally spilling out of the baskets in the upstairs hallway, smelling damp—and I was paralyzed. I ended up having to call a plumber, a very nice man named Gary, who charged me sixty-five pounds just to come out and pull a stray button out of the filter. Sixty-five pounds! Because I was too terrified to walk down a flight of stairs. 

And the garden... oh, the garden is a whole other story. We have this lovely old shed at the back, where we keep the lawnmower and the shears and the potting soil. But it's damp, and it's dark, and it is prime spider territory. I haven't been in there since last summer after I saw one the size of a saucer—well, maybe not a saucer, but it was enormous, I swear to you—sitting on the handle of the spade. Now, I have to hire a local boy, Tommy from three streets over, to come and mow the lawn and do the weeding, because I refuse to go into the shed to get the tools. 

So, yes, owning this house has become significantly more expensive and just... harder to manage. Chores get backed up, I'm paying for help I shouldn't need, and I'm completely avoiding parts of my own property. It makes me feel terribly foolish, and I know my husband gets frustrated, even if he tries not to show it, because he ends up having to pick up the slack when he's already working such long hours. It's really taking a toll on how we live in our own home.

Well, as I was just saying a moment ago about my husband, yes, it absolutely does. I know I feel like I’m repeating myself a bit, but it all really ties back to the situation with the house, you see. Because owning this property has become so much more expensive and just generally harder to manage, all because I’m paying for small maintenance help, letting chores back up, and completely avoiding parts of the property I actually need to use. My husband, bless him, he tries to be patient. But when he comes home from a twelve-hour shift at the hospital, the last thing he wants to do is go down to the basement to fetch the laundry because I've let it pile up for days, or go out to the damp shed to get the folding chairs when we have friends over for a barbecue in the garden. It causes tension, it really does. We bicker about it. He’ll sigh, or he’ll roll his eyes, and I feel terribly guilty, but I also feel defensive because I literally cannot help it! And the money I'm spending on people like Tommy or the plumber—that’s money we could be putting toward a nice holiday in Cornwall or a nice dinner out together, but instead, it's going toward things we shouldn't have to pay for, which frustrates him no end.

And it affects my wider family, too. I mentioned my sister, Susan, who visits from Canada. We were supposed to have that loft converted into a guest suite for her by now. She comes over every other Christmas, and we used to have such a lovely time, but because I can't even go up there to clear the boxes out, it's just sitting there empty. So she has to sleep on the pull-out sofa in the study, which is dreadful for her back—she has terrible sciatica, poor thing. Last time she was here, she actually made a comment about how she might just book a room at the Premier Inn down the road next year. It absolutely broke my heart. She’s too polite to make a big fuss, but I know she feels put out. 

Even with friends... it's embarrassing to explain to people why you can't just nip into your own shed to grab a trowel, or why you're paying a neighborhood boy to do something you're perfectly physically capable of doing yourself. So, yes, it’s not just a silly little fear that I keep to myself. It’s actively making me a burden to my husband and a worse hostess to my sister, all because I can't manage my own home properly.

Not like having to tap the doorframe three times or wash my hands a certain number of ways, if that's what you mean. I mean, I suppose you could say my \"ritual\" is just staying as far away as humanly possible from anywhere a spider might be. \n\nLike, if I have to go into a room where I haven't been in a while, I don't do a little dance or repeat a phrase, I just... don't go in. Or I make my husband do it, if he's home, which he isn't always because of his shifts at the hospital, and then I just have to wait. But I don't have a routine I go through to make the fear go away. I just try to make sure I never put myself in a position where the fear happens in the first place. Which, as I was saying about the laundry, is becoming completely unmanageable. I mean, you can only buy so many new pairs of socks before it starts to get ridiculous, right? And I refuse to be the woman who buys new underwear just to avoid the basement, but I swear I’ve been tempted. So, no rituals, no repeating things. Just a lot of running away.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself thinking about spiders when you're not trying to?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not exactly. I mean, it’s not like I’m just sitting there in the staff room at school, having a cup of tea and marking papers, and suddenly I’m obsessing over spiders for absolutely no reason. It doesn't really work like that for me. \n\nWhen I'm teaching—I teach history, mostly to the older students—my mind is completely on the lesson. You really have to be on your toes with teenagers, you know? You can't just let your mind wander or lose your focus, or they'll completely derail the class. So during the day, if I'm in a safe environment like my classroom or my living room, they don't just pop into my head uninvited. I'm not plagued by thoughts of them out of the blue. \n\nNow, if I know I have to go somewhere they might be... well, that’s a different story entirely. Like, if I know it’s Sunday afternoon and I absolutely have to wash my blouses for the work week, then yes, I will spend hours dreading it. I'll be sitting on the sofa, trying to watch a program, but in the back of my mind, I'm just thinking, \"I have to go down there soon. What if there's one on the stairs? What if it's right above the washing machine?\" But I feel like that's only because I know I have to face that specific space, if you see what I mean. \n\nIf I don't have to go near the basement, or the shed, or the garage, I don't think about them at all. I just want to live my life normally. So as long as I don't have a reason to think one is nearby, my mind is completely clear of them. It's definitely not a constant, nagging thought when I'm just going about a normal, safe day.\n\nDoctor: How would you describe the level of anxiety or fear you feel when you think about encountering a spider?\n\nPatient: Well, it’s... it’s completely out of proportion, and I know that. I mean, rationally, logically, as an educated woman, I know a spider in the corner of an old house probably isn’t going to hurt me. I live in England, for goodness' sake, we don't exactly have deadly tarantulas roaming the countryside. I tell myself this all the time. I say, \"Margaret, it's just a tiny little thing, it's more afraid of you than you are of it.\" You know, all the standard things people say. \n\nBut the moment I actually picture one... like, if I just imagine one dropping out of a cardboard box when I'm trying to get the Christmas decorations down, or just sitting there, completely still, on the wall near the washing machine... the fear is just overwhelming. It feels enormous. It feels incredibly threatening, in a way that I am, frankly, quite embarrassed to admit to you. My heart starts hammering against my ribs like I've just run a marathon, my palms get sweaty, and I feel this absolute, desperate need to just get away. It's not a mild dislike. It's not like, \"Oh, yuck, a bug.\" It's a sudden, intense panic, like I'm in actual, physical danger. And it's so frustrating because my brain—my logical brain—is sitting there going, \"This is ridiculous,\" but my body is reacting as if there's a tiger in the room. It just takes over completely.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your fear of spiders is something that you're unable to control?\n\nPatient: Well, yes and no. I mean, I suppose I can control it in the sense that I control my environment, right? Like I said, I just don't go down to the basement anymore. If I don't go where they are, I don't have the fear, so in a roundabout way, I'm controlling it by just avoiding it entirely. Which, as I've mentioned, is becoming a logistical nightmare with the laundry, and I really don't know how much longer I can keep asking my husband to fetch things for me, especially when he's just come off a twelve-hour shift at the hospital and he's completely exhausted. It's not fair to him, and it makes me feel terribly guilty. \n\nBut if you mean controlling the fear when it actually happens... when I'm faced with one, or even when I just think I might be? No. Not at all. I have absolutely zero control over it. It's like someone flips a switch in my brain and all the logic and reason I have just completely vanishes. I've tried, you know. I've stood at the top of the basement stairs and gripped the banister and told myself, \"Margaret, you are a fifty-four-year-old woman with a university degree, you manage a classroom of thirty rowdy teenagers every single day, you can walk down a flight of wooden stairs.\" And I'll take a breath, and I'll try to force myself to just take that first step. \n\nBut I can't. My legs literally won't move. My chest gets tight, and I just start picturing them scurrying out from under the steps or dropping from the ceiling, and before I know it, I'm backing away and shutting the door as fast as I can. It's like my body just completely overrides my mind. It's humiliating, really, to feel so entirely powerless over something so small. So, no, when the fear hits, I am completely at its mercy. I just have to run away until it passes.\n\nDoctor: Is your fear specifically of spiders or does it extend to other insects or creatures as well?\n\nPatient: Well, no, it's really just the spiders. I mean, I don't love other bugs, obviously. I don't think anyone really enjoys finding a woodlouse under a plant pot or a moth fluttering around the lampshade when you're trying to read in the evening. Just last week, actually, I was sitting in the conservatory—which is lovely this time of year, we just had the glass cleaned—and a rather large bluebottle fly got trapped inside. It was buzzing against the window, making that awful racket they make, and I found it annoying, certainly. I had to get a magazine—I think it was a copy of *Country Life*—and sort of waft it toward the open door until it finally got the hint and left. But I wasn't afraid of it. I didn't feel that horrible, gripping panic in my chest. I just thought, \"Oh, what a nuisance.\" \n\nEven bees or wasps, which I know some people are quite terrified of because they can sting you... I respect them, certainly. If a wasp comes near my jam sandwich when we're having a picnic in the park, I'll sit very still and wait for it to move on, or I'll calmly pack up the food. I don't want to be stung, naturally. But I don't lose my mind over it. I don't feel like I have to flee the park entirely and never go back. \n\nBut spiders... it's just them. There's something about the way they look, the way they move. Those long, spindly legs and how they scuttle so fast, or worse, how they just sit there, completely motionless, like they're waiting for you. It's just them. If I found a beetle in the basement, I'd probably just sweep it up with the dustpan and brush and toss it outside without a second thought. But if I saw a spider down there... well, as I've said, I wouldn't even be down there in the first place, but if I were, I'd be halfway down the street before I even realized I was running. So, yes, it's very specific. Just the spiders. Nothing else gives me that awful, dreadful feeling.\n\nDoctor: Are there any significant areas of your life, such as relationships or work, that are being affected by your fear of spiders?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, absolutely. It's... it's becoming quite a problem, actually, and it's mostly around the house. My husband and I bought this beautiful older property about five years ago—it's a lovely Victorian terrace, lots of character, original fireplaces, that sort of thing. But older houses, well, they require upkeep. And they have... spaces. Nooks and crannies. The basement, obviously, which I've already told you about, but also the loft. \n\nWe have this enormous loft space, and we were planning to convert it into a lovely little guest suite for when my sister visits from Canada, but I can't even bring myself to go up there to clear out the old boxes because I just know, I *know*, it's going to be absolutely crawling with them. So, the loft sits empty and useless. \n\nAnd it's not just avoiding spaces, it's the cost. It's actually costing us money, which is ridiculous. Just last month, the washing machine—which is in the basement, of course—started making this dreadful clanking noise. Normally, I'd just pop down, check the filter, maybe see if a coin got stuck, you know? But I couldn't. I couldn't go down there. My husband was away at a medical conference in Edinburgh, so I couldn't ask him. The laundry was piling up—literally spilling out of the baskets in the upstairs hallway, smelling damp—and I was paralyzed. I ended up having to call a plumber, a very nice man named Gary, who charged me sixty-five pounds just to come out and pull a stray button out of the filter. Sixty-five pounds! Because I was too terrified to walk down a flight of stairs. \n\nAnd the garden... oh, the garden is a whole other story. We have this lovely old shed at the back, where we keep the lawnmower and the shears and the potting soil. But it's damp, and it's dark, and it is prime spider territory. I haven't been in there since last summer after I saw one the size of a saucer—well, maybe not a saucer, but it was enormous, I swear to you—sitting on the handle of the spade. Now, I have to hire a local boy, Tommy from three streets over, to come and mow the lawn and do the weeding, because I refuse to go into the shed to get the tools. \n\nSo, yes, owning this house has become significantly more expensive and just... harder to manage. Chores get backed up, I'm paying for help I shouldn't need, and I'm completely avoiding parts of my own property. It makes me feel terribly foolish, and I know my husband gets frustrated, even if he tries not to show it, because he ends up having to pick up the slack when he's already working such long hours. It's really taking a toll on how we live in our own home.\n\nDoctor: Has your fear of spiders affected your relationships with friends or family members in any way?\n\nPatient: Well, as I was just saying a moment ago about my husband, yes, it absolutely does. I know I feel like I’m repeating myself a bit, but it all really ties back to the situation with the house, you see. Because owning this property has become so much more expensive and just generally harder to manage, all because I’m paying for small maintenance help, letting chores back up, and completely avoiding parts of the property I actually need to use. And you can imagine how that spills over into my relationships. \n\nMy husband, bless him, he tries to be patient. But when he comes home from a twelve-hour shift at the hospital, the last thing he wants to do is go down to the basement to fetch the laundry because I've let it pile up for days, or go out to the damp shed to get the folding chairs when we have friends over for a barbecue in the garden. It causes tension, it really does. We bicker about it. He’ll sigh, or he’ll roll his eyes, and I feel terribly guilty, but I also feel defensive because I literally cannot help it! And the money I'm spending on people like Tommy or the plumber—that’s money we could be putting toward a nice holiday in Cornwall or a nice dinner out together, but instead, it's going toward things we shouldn't have to pay for, which frustrates him no end.\n\nAnd it affects my wider family, too. I mentioned my sister, Susan, who visits from Canada. We were supposed to have that loft converted into a guest suite for her by now. She comes over every other Christmas, and we used to have such a lovely time, but because I can't even go up there to clear the boxes out, it's just sitting there empty. So she has to sleep on the pull-out sofa in the study, which is dreadful for her back—she has terrible sciatica, poor thing. Last time she was here, she actually made a comment about how she might just book a room at the Premier Inn down the road next year. It absolutely broke my heart. She’s too polite to make a big fuss, but I know she feels put out. \n\nEven with friends... it's embarrassing to explain to people why you can't just nip into your own shed to grab a trowel, or why you're paying a neighborhood boy to do something you're perfectly physically capable of doing yourself. So, yes, it’s not just a silly little fear that I keep to myself. Well, as for traveling, I suppose... I mean, I absolutely refuse to go camping, if that counts. A few years ago, my husband suggested we try one of those glamping holidays in the Lake District—you know, staying in a yurt with a little wood-burning stove and all that? I just looked at him and laughed. Imagine the spiders in a damp canvas yurt! And at work—I'm a secondary school teacher—I always manage to wriggle out of chaperoning the Duke of Edinburgh outdoor expeditions. I usually tell the headmaster my knees can't take the hiking, which is a little white lie, but really, it's the sheer terror of unzipping a tent in the middle of a field and finding a massive spider sitting on my sleeping bag. So yes, I do avoid those sorts of activities. 

But honestly, Doctor, missing out on a camping trip or a school hike isn't the end of the world. What really brings me in here to see you today, the absolute breaking point for me, is that I keep arranging my own house around not seeing spiders. It's exactly what I've been going on about—I put off the laundry in the basement until it's a crisis, I completely avoid the garden shed, and I'm even paying people to do these small, ridiculous jobs that I know perfectly well how to do myself. 

I'm an educated, capable woman! I know how to clear a washing machine filter. I know how to fetch a lawnmower and weed a flowerbed. But I just... I can’t make myself go into those spaces. It’s one thing to avoid a forest or a campsite, but having to navigate my own home like it’s a minefield, constantly plotting how to avoid the basement or the loft or the shed... it’s just become entirely unmanageable. Well, aside from what we've already discussed... let me think. No, not really. I mean, if I'm just going about my normal day outside the house, I'm absolutely fine. Well, hobbies... let me think. I mean, if we exclude the camping and the hiking that I mentioned earlier—which, to be perfectly honest, were never really my cup of tea to begin with, even before the spider issue got this bad. My job? Teaching? Oh, goodness, no. I think I touched on this a moment ago, but the school is absolutely fine. I can stand up there and teach the Tudors or the World Wars without a single worry. The classroom is practically my sanctuary at this point. 

But... if you're asking about how it impacts my ability to function in a broader sense, like my "job" of running my own life, well, that's where the real toll is. It’s the house. Sections I *need* to use! I have this lovely, spacious house, and I'm practically living in half of it, paying a premium out of a teacher's salary to keep the other half ticking over without me having to step foot in the damp corners. It’s just exhausting, Doctor, and so incredibly frustrating to feel like a hostage to your own floorplan.

I just have to run away until it passes.\n\nDoctor: Is your fear specifically of spiders or does it extend to other insects or creatures as well?\n\nPatient: Well, no, it's really just the spiders. Friends and colleagues? Oh, no. No, I wouldn't say so at all. In fact, my social life is quite untouched by the whole ordeal, thankfully. 

You see, with my colleagues at the school—and I know I keep bringing the school up, but it really is my safe haven—we just interact in the staff room or the corridors. I suppose... well, if I really think about it, the only minor change is that I don't host them at my house for garden parties anymore. So, the relationships themselves are absolutely fine, they haven't suffered a bit. I just manage the logistics of where we meet so I don't have to worry about anything creeping out from under a patio chair and causing me to make a scene. It feels enormous. It feels incredibly threatening, in a way that I am, frankly, quite embarrassed to admit to you. My heart starts hammering against my ribs like I've just run a marathon, my palms get sweaty, and I feel this absolute, desperate need to just get away. It's not a mild dislike. It's not like, \"Oh, yuck, a bug.\" It's a sudden, intense panic, like I'm in actual, physical danger. And it's so frustrating because my brain—my logical brain—is sitting there going, \"This is ridiculous,\" but my body is reacting as if there's a tiger in the room. It just takes over completely.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your fear of spiders is something that you're unable to control?\n\nPatient: Well, yes and no. I mean, I suppose I can control it in the sense that I control my environment, right? Like I said, I just don't go down to the basement anymore. If I don't go where they are, I don't have the fear, so in a roundabout way, I'm controlling it by just avoiding it entirely. My legs literally won't move. My chest gets tight, and I just start picturing them scurrying out from under the steps or dropping from the ceiling, and before I know it, I'm backing away and shutting the door as fast as I can. And at work—I'm a secondary school teacher—I always manage to wriggle out of chaperoning the Duke of Edinburgh outdoor expeditions. I usually tell the headmaster my knees can't take the hiking, which is a little white lie, but really, it's the sheer terror of unzipping a tent in the middle of a field and finding a massive spider sitting on my sleeping bag. So yes, I do avoid those sorts of activities. \n\nBut honestly, Doctor, missing out on a camping trip or a school hike isn't the end of the world. What really brings me in here to see you today, the absolute breaking point for me, is that I keep arranging my own house around not seeing spiders. It's exactly what I've been going on about—I put off the laundry in the basement until it's a crisis, I completely avoid the garden shed, and I'm even paying people to do these small, ridiculous jobs that I know perfectly well how to do myself. \n\nI'm an educated, capable woman! I know how to clear a washing machine filter. I know how to fetch a lawnmower and weed a flowerbed. But I just... I can’t make myself go into those spaces. It’s one thing to avoid a forest or a campsite, but having to navigate my own home like it’s a minefield, constantly plotting how to avoid the basement or the loft or the shed... it’s just become entirely unmanageable. It's exhausting having to map out my daily life just to ensure I don't cross paths with one, and I just can't go on living in my own home this way.\n\nDoctor: Are there any daily activities or tasks, aside from those involving specific places like the basement or shed, that you find yourself struggling with or avoiding due to your fear of spiders?\n\nPatient: Well, aside from what we've already discussed... let me think. No, not really. I mean, if I'm just going about my normal day outside the house, I'm absolutely fine. I drive to the school every morning—I teach Year 9 and 10 history, which, as you can imagine, takes up a tremendous amount of mental energy just keeping thirty teenagers focused on the Industrial Revolution. But the school building itself is quite modern, very bright and well-kept, so I never really worry about encountering anything there. I don't struggle with the grocery shopping at Tesco, or popping down to the high street to go to the bank, or anything like that. \n\nSo, no, it's not as if I can't function in the wider world. Which is exactly why this whole situation is so utterly maddening! I can stand up in front of a classroom and command the attention of dozens of adolescents, I can organize a term's worth of curriculum, I can run my errands perfectly well... but the moment I cross the threshold of my own home, it’s a different story entirely. I can sit at the kitchen table and grade essays for hours without a second thought, but if I need to step near the cellar door just to put the recycling out, my heart just stops. \n\nIt really, truly does just come back to those specific spaces in the house—the damp areas, the dark areas, the nooks and crannies I was telling you about earlier. If it were everywhere, I suppose I'd never leave my bed! But because it's so localized to the basement, the loft, and the shed, it just feels like this ridiculous trap I've set for myself by buying a Victorian property. So aside from the property maintenance and the chores tied to those exact spots, no, my everyday activities aren't really affected. Well, I know we keep circling back to this, and I really do feel quite silly bringing it up yet again—you must think I have absolutely nothing else going on in my life!—but it truly is the day-to-day running of my home. That is the situation where I am just... well, completely impaired, to use your word. 

Owning this house, which I used to love so dearly, has just become so terribly expensive and so much harder to manage, all because of this fear. It’s the mundane activities that cause the most distress. For instance, just last week, a lightbulb went out in the stairwell leading down to the cellar. Now, any normal person would just pop down, unscrew the old one, and put in a new one. But I simply couldn't. I stood at the top of those stairs, looking into the dim light, knowing full well the sorts of webs that gather in those corners, and I just froze. I ended up having to call Martin, a local handyman from the village, to come and change a simple lightbulb. He charged me thirty-five pounds! I am constantly paying out of pocket for small maintenance help like that, and it is absolutely draining my finances. 

And because I can't do these things, I’m just letting chores back up for weeks on end. The recycling is a perfect example. The bins are kept round the back, near the ivy, and I refuse to go near the ivy after a rather nasty fright I had last summer. So, the cardboard boxes and the tin cans just pile up in the kitchen until I can convince my sister to take them out when she visits, or until I pay Martin to do a garden clearance.
